title: Progressive stiffness with a family pattern

blocks.text: Progressive stiffness with a family pattern

AMaC MRCP PACES · R5-174 · Neurological examination · PACES Station 3, neurological examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 examination, at least 4 questions) · Guideline dates and links in section 15 · Related AMaC: condition may appear elsewhere in a different context

Dear Doctor, examine the lower limbs and gait of a woman aged 41, who has slowly progressive stiffness. Localise the findings, discuss the differential and outline further assessment. She usually uses a stick; check safety before standing. You may request relevant upper-limb, cranial-nerve and investigation findings.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK: A predominantly pyramidal leg syndrome with a family history raises hereditary spastic paraplegia.
TRAP: A family history is not permission to skip treatable acquired causes or to invent a specific gene and inheritance risk.

rows: “Please relax while I check stiffness and then strength.”
Assess velocity-dependent tone, power, reflexes, clonus and plantar responses.
“I would check for other neurological features before calling this uncomplicated.”
Assess sensation and request cranial, upper-limb, cerebellar and cognitive findings.
“Who else has had walking stiffness, and at what age?”
Build a brief pedigree without assuming all relatives have the same diagnosis.
“An inherited condition is possible; we should also exclude treatable alternatives.”
Review imaging and targeted blood tests, then coordinate neurology, genetics and rehabilitation.
Walks the patient without her stick.
Assesses supported gait after checking stability.
Uses walking observations to guide examination without increasing fall risk.
Finds leg spasticity, hyperreflexia and extensor plantars.
Describes a symmetrical pyramidal pattern with relatively modest weakness.
Looks for a sensory level and distal modalities.
Screens for complex features and avoids over-localising from one negative test.
Declares a named gene from bedside signs.
Retains cord compression, inflammatory and metabolic alternatives despite the pedigree.
Plans neurology assessment and appropriate counselling.
Explains diagnostic versus predictive testing and respects relatives’ autonomy.
Promises all children will be unaffected.
Addresses falls, bladder symptoms, work goals and shared rehabilitation priorities.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade.
Skills: A physical examination; B identifying physical signs; C clinical communication; D differential diagnosis; E clinical judgement; F managing patients’ concerns; G maintaining patient welfare.

Patient: a librarian, with eight years of gradually stiff legs and increasing toe scuffing. No abrupt attacks, major back pain, sensory level symptoms or visual loss. Your father developed a stiff walk in middle age and a paternal aunt uses walking aids; neither has a confirmed genetic diagnosis. You have urinary urgency without current retention or recurrent infection.

Only if asked: no arm weakness, choking, cognitive change or seizures. A recent brain and whole-spine MRI found no explanatory structural lesion. B12 and copper testing were normal; other testing is being considered by neurology according to history. You take prescribed antispasticity treatment and attend physiotherapy. No allergies. Your concern is what this means for your teenage son. Say, “Can you tell from my legs whether he will get this?” Accept uncertainty if the candidate explains the purpose of counselling; do not consent to testing your son on his behalf.

Findings and delivery. Walking with a stick shows a stiff, narrow-based gait with toe scuffing. There is bilateral lower-limb spasticity, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, ankle clonus and extensor plantar responses. Hip flexion and ankle dorsiflexion are mildly weak, approximately MRC 4/5; other leg groups are near normal. No definite truncal sensory level; light touch and pinprick are preserved, with mildly reduced vibration at the toes. Upper-limb examination, eye movements and cerebellar testing are normal on request. No wasting, fasciculation or bulbar signs are supplied. The bedside pattern suggests a predominantly leg pyramidal syndrome; it does not identify the genetic subtype.

Question ladder. Q1 (R4) Where is the problem? Bilateral corticospinal pathways affecting the legs; the examination alone does not establish a single precise structural level. Q2 (R4) What makes hereditary disease plausible? A slow course, predominantly leg pyramidal signs and similarly affected relatives are supportive, after acquired causes have been assessed. Q3 (R3) What makes a complex phenotype? Additional neuropathy, ataxia, cognitive change, seizures or other neurological/systemic features may suggest a complex form or an alternative diagnosis. Q4 (R5) What testing would you discuss? Review spinal/brain imaging and targeted investigations for acquired causes. If unexplained, offer specialist genomic assessment with consent and counselling through the relevant national pathway. Q5 (R6) What can you tell her son? A specific risk requires a family diagnosis and inheritance assessment. Predictive testing is a separate decision for the relative, with age-appropriate specialist counselling.
Distinguishes spasticity from other increased tone (A B).
Looks for a sensory level and extra-leg features (A D).
Uses the pedigree without skipping acquired causes (D).
Discusses testing and family implications without invented certainty (E G).
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: “Your father has it, so your son definitely will.” [R6 Fail] Orders a single named gene without reviewing imaging or counselling. [R4 Fail R5 Fail]
Pass performance

CANDIDATE demonstrates a spastic paraparesis, asks about sensory and other neurological features and considers hereditary spastic paraplegia within a wider differential. [R2 Pass R3 Pass R4 Pass] Plans specialist genetics and rehabilitation. [R5 Pass]
High-performance performance

CANDIDATE distinguishes a clinical suspicion from molecular confirmation and diagnostic testing from a relative’s predictive choice. [R4 High R5 High] Balances the family concern with the patient’s immediate walking and bladder goals. [R6 High] EXAMINER: protects against both missed treatable disease and premature genetic claims.
R3: A sensory level would change the differential and cannot be assumed absent without assessment.
R4: The bedside examination cannot distinguish all HSP subtypes.
R6: Genetic information concerns relatives but does not remove their right to decide about testing.
“An inherited cause is plausible, but I must check what has been excluded.”
“I cannot give your son’s risk without establishing the family diagnosis.”
“Let us separate the diagnostic question from what would improve walking now.”

Hereditary spastic paraplegia comprises genetically heterogeneous conditions, with pure and complex phenotypes and several inheritance patterns. Absence of a family history does not exclude it, and a positive pedigree does not exclude acquired cord disease. Genomic eligibility and testing arrangements differ by nation and should be confirmed through the local specialist service. Do not equate one uncertain variant with a confirmed diagnosis. Physiotherapy, mobility aids, bladder assessment and individualised spasticity care can proceed while the cause is investigated.
THINK: Chronic spastic paraparesis plus a pedigree raises, but does not prove, HSP.
SAY: “We should look for both inherited and treatable acquired causes.”
DO: Pyramidal signs, sensation, gait and complex-feature screen.
NUMBERS: Give no inheritance percentage without the molecular/family context.
TRAP: Genetics before excluding acquired causes.
FINISH: Neurology, counselling and practical rehabilitation goals.
